candidates.name: Raw log line to event template with parameter masking (Loghub-2.0)
candidates.industry: IT operations / AIOps; industrial and transport system logs (HDFS, BGL, Thunderbird, Spark, OpenSSH and others)
candidates.task: Input: one raw log line. Output: a template string with variable fields replaced by placeholders (e.g. <*>), plus the event ID that groups it with other lines from the same template.
candidates.why_hard_for_llm: Frontier-class LLMs parse templates imperfectly, and the errors are silent. The best published LLM-based parser reports parsing accuracy (PA) of 84.2 (ChatGPT, gpt-3.5-turbo-0613) on average, so about 16% of templates are not matched exactly. The task also has many datasets with 11 to 1,241 templates each, which a prompt cannot cover in full. Caveat: the LLM parsers that do best already use retrieved in-context examples (LILAC, DivLog), so the problem is partly solved by retrieval.
candidates.business_value: Operations and SRE teams that run log-based anomaly detection or incident search. Accurate templates make counts, alerts and dashboards stable. A small local model removes per-line API cost on high-volume logs (Loghub-2.0 averages about 3.6 million lines per dataset).

datasets.name: Loghub-2.0 (14 system log collections, annotated templates)
datasets.size: 14 datasets, 3,601,187 annotated logs on average per dataset, 249.1 templates on average (GitHub README table, fetched 2026-10-29); full data on Zenodo, 965.6 MB in 14 zip files
datasets.labels: Ground-truth template per line (EventTemplate); a sample of 2k lines per system exists as Loghub-2k
datasets.license: CC BY 4.0 (Zenodo record 8275861, fetched). The GitHub page links a LICENSE file but its text was not read.
datasets.notes: Zenodo record 8275861 published 2023-08-23. The GitHub README table lists 14 rows, so 14 is the count used here. The ISSTA 2024 LogPub paper is the citation the licence asks for. Log anomaly labels were not checked in this pass.

datasets.name: Loghub-2k (2,000-line samples per system)
datasets.size: 2k lines per system (not re-read in this pass)
datasets.notes: Smaller sample for quick iteration. Only the Loghub-2.0 page was fetched.

frontier_evidence.source: LILAC: Log Parsing using LLMs with Adaptive Parsing Cache (FSE 2024)
frontier_evidence.models_tested: ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613), Davinci, Curie. No GPT-4 or newer model reported.
frontier_evidence.finding: Average over datasets, from Table 4 (arXiv HTML): ChatGPT GA 92.7 / PA 84.2; Davinci GA 91.9 / PA 87.1; Curie GA 90.1 / PA 77.8.

frontier_evidence.source: A Comparative Study on Large Language Models for Log Parsing (ESEM 2024)
frontier_evidence.models_tested: GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613), Claude 2.1, Llama 2 7B, CodeLlama 7B, Zephyr 7B, CodeUp 13B; zero-shot and four-shot
frontier_evidence.finding: Few-shot, 1,354 unique messages from LogHub: CodeLlama 586 correct, GPT-3.5 531, Claude 2.1 439 (counts from Table 3). The abstract's 10% gap is 586 against 531. These are template-extraction counts, not F1.

frontier_evidence.source: LibreLog (arXiv 2408.01585) reports LILAC baseline on Loghub-2.0
frontier_evidence.models_tested: LILAC run with Llama3-8B, because the authors replaced ChatGPT for a fair comparison
frontier_evidence.finding: Average on LogHub-2.0 for LILAC: GA 0.8289, PA 0.6783 (Table I). This is a baseline from a competing paper, and the authors are the ones who built LibreLog.

frontier_evidence.source: Small is Beautiful: A Practical and Efficient Log Parsing Framework (arXiv 2601.22590)
frontier_evidence.models_tested: GPT-3.5 for the reference row; Gemini-1.5-Flash-8B (default), LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen3 4B/8B/14B for robustness
frontier_evidence.finding: Average on Loghub-2.0 (Table 3): GPT-3.5 GA 92.3 / PA 88.0; Gemini-8B GA 92.2 / PA 88.9. The paper's text gives a different GA figure from its table. The table is used here.

counterevidence.note: Non-LLM Drain scores GA 0.8432 average on LogHub-2.0, above LILAC (0.8289), though its PA is 0.4681. An LLM is not needed to get grouping right; the LLM mainly helps PA. This weakens the claim that frontier LLMs are unreliable at grouping.

A fine-tuned or prompted 8B-class model reaches GA about 92 on Loghub-2.0, close to GPT-3.5. Once a small model is adequate, the frontier gap is small, so the case for fine-tuning must rest on PA, cost and latency, not on accuracy above frontier.

counterevidence.source: DivLog (training-free in-context parsing, 2023) as reported in a 2025 comparison
counterevidence.note: Reported figures of 98.1% PA on average for GPT-3 (not re-read). Unverified; if correct, retrieved examples close most of the gap, which means RAG-style fixes may suffice.

small_model_evidence.source: LibreLog: open 8B model with unsupervised parsing
small_model_evidence.finding: Llama3-8B-based LibreLog: average GA 0.8720, PA 0.8538 on LogHub-2.0 (Table I), above the LILAC baseline run with the same model (GA 0.8289, PA 0.6783). This is an unsupervised, open-weight 8B result from the paper's authors.

small_model_evidence.source: LLMParser (fine-tuned T5-base, cited as a baseline in LibreLog Table I)
small_model_evidence.finding: A fine-tuned small model with the lowest grouping in that table: GA 0.6345, PA 0.7514 average on LogHub-2.0. This is a warning: a fine-tuned small model can parse well and still group poorly.

candidates.why_ft_beats_rag: Weak claim for this task. The top LLM parsers already use retrieved examples (LILAC, DivLog), and a deterministic parser (Drain) is competitive on grouping. Fine-tuning beats RAG only if a retrieval-plus-LLM baseline is run and still misses on held-out log systems. This has to be tested, not assumed.
candidates.example_input: 081109 203615 148 INFO dfs.DataNode$PacketResponder: PacketResponder 1 for block blk_-1608999687919862906 terminating
candidates.example_output: dfs.DataNode$PacketResponder: PacketResponder <*> for block <*> terminating  (event template with the block ID and counter masked)
candidates.behavior_spec: Given one raw log line, the model returns a template in which every variable token (IDs, numbers, paths, addresses) is replaced by <*>, and the template string matches the ground truth exactly for at least 95% of lines on a held-out system. Output is valid JSON with no prose.
candidates.agentic_demo: Step 1: a log collector pulls lines from a source (file or syslog). Step 2: the SLM returns template and event ID per line, validated by regex (no unmasked digits or hex). Step 3: a counting tool groups lines by template and flags a new template as an anomaly. Step 4: an incident-search tool queries events by template ID. Tools are plain code; the model only does the masking.
candidates.eval: Parsing accuracy (PA) and grouping accuracy (GA) as in the Loghub papers, computed by the official LogPAI evaluation scripts on held-out Loghub-2.0 systems. Compare base 1.7B-4B, tuned, Drain (non-LLM) and one frontier model on the same lines. Add a held-out system not in training to test generalisation.
candidates.risks: The benchmark is solved by retrieval and by deterministic tools, so the case is not clear. Most public results use GPT-3.5 or older 7-8B models; GPT-4-class or newer results were not found. Loghub is synthetic-looking and public, so training leakage risk exists if the model was pre-trained on Loghub.
candidates.qlora_feasibility: Fits 4 days. Data is ready (Zenodo CC BY 4.0 zip files, no gate). Labelled pairs are generated by the ground truth. Main effort is slicing 3.6 million lines per dataset to a training set of a few thousand, with a per-system split.

candidates.name: NASA ASRS aviation safety report coding (phase of flight and contributing factors)
candidates.industry: Aviation (airlines, safety offices, regulators); transport safety
candidates.task: Input: one ASRS narrative (free-text incident report). Output: a structured record with the flight phase (e.g. Taxi, Takeoff, Initial Climb, Cruise, Descent, Final Approach, Landing) and one or more contributing-factor labels from the ASRS taxonomy.
candidates.why_hard_for_llm: Labels follow the ASRS coding taxonomy, which is specific and inconsistent with everyday usage (for example, what counts as a human-factors cause). The fine-tuned domain encoder SafeAeroBERT beat BERT on Procedure and Weather (0.845 vs 0.766; 0.871 vs 0.807) but did worse on Human Factors (0.549 vs 0.608). No frontier LLM result on the same label set was found in this pass, so the claim that LLMs are unreliable here is hypothetical until tested.
candidates.business_value: Airline and general aviation safety analysts code thousands of reports by hand. Consistent coding feeds trend analysis, safety-case evidence and regulator reporting. A local model keeps sensitive narratives in-house, which matters for reports that identify people.

datasets.name: NASA ASRS database (search interface and report requests)
datasets.size: Not verified in this pass (the public search interface is the only documented access)
datasets.labels: Official ASRS coding fields: flight phase, anomaly, contributing factors (per the ASRS coding taxonomy)
datasets.license: Not verified. NASA's Requesting ASRS Data page gives no licence, public-domain statement or terms of use; access is by a contact-form request, subject to program resources.
datasets.notes: Bulk export is by request, not by download. Ask the ASRS office for a statement of need before relying on it. The NASA page says the database is available to interested parties.

datasets.name: elihoole/asrs-aviation-reports (Hugging Face)
datasets.size: 47.7k rows: train 38.7k, validation 4.3k, test 4.77k (dataset card, fetched)
datasets.labels: Visible fields include Aircraft 1.9_Flight Phase and Person 1.7_Human Factors. No visible contributing-factor or anomaly column in the first part of the viewer; the list was truncated.
datasets.license: apache-2.0 (dataset card, fetched). Underlying NASA terms for this copy not verified.
datasets.notes: Good for a flight-phase pilot. Check the full column list before use. Treat the Apache-2.0 tag as the repacker's licence, not NASA's.

datasets.name: ASRS-ChatGPT (archanatikayatray, Hugging Face)
datasets.labels: Analyst synopsis and human-factors labels (human-factors subset only)
datasets.notes: Narrow subset of human-factors problems. Not general enough for a contributing-factor task.

datasets.name: SIAM 2007 Text Mining Competition aviation safety reports (ASRS-derived)
datasets.size: Test set 7,077 documents (NASP-T paper, Table 1 source; full corpus size not stated)
datasets.labels: Multi-label problem categories (examples: Engine Problem, Cabin Pressure Problem, Navigation Problem)
datasets.notes: A labelled benchmark used by a 2025 paper, but no frontier LLM was tested on it. Find the original source before use.

frontier_evidence.source: Tikayat Ray et al., ChatGPT for ASRS incident synopses and human-factors identification (Aerospace 2023)
frontier_evidence.finding: Reported precision 0.61 on human-factors identification (from a search summary; the MDPI page returned HTTP 403 and was not read).

frontier_evidence.source: No frontier-LLM study on ASRS contributing-factor labels found (2024-2025)
frontier_evidence.finding: Several searches for GPT-4 or Claude results on ASRS coding found no paper. The gap is itself a finding: the prompt-ceiling gate would need to be the first experiment here.

counterevidence.note: Shows that a domain-tuned encoder does not win on every label: Human Factors accuracy is 0.549 for SafeAeroBERT against 0.608 for BERT. Some labels are harder for any model.

counterevidence.source: Human-factors labels in the ASRS-ChatGPT subset
counterevidence.note: Not re-read. Fine-tuned models may not beat frontier models on human-factors judgments, which are subjective.

small_model_evidence.source: SafeAeroBERT: 2023 AIAA Aviation paper (Andrade and Walsh)
small_model_evidence.finding: Model card table (accuracy): Procedure BERT 0.766, SafeAeroBERT 0.845; Weather BERT 0.807, SafeAeroBERT 0.871; Aircraft BERT 0.747, SafeAeroBERT 0.740; Human Factors BERT 0.608, SafeAeroBERT 0.549. These are encoder models trained on ASRS and NTSB text, not small generative LLMs. Model card says its figures may come from an earlier version.

small_model_evidence.source: NASP-T: Fuzzy Neuro-Symbolic Transformer for aviation safety report classification
small_model_evidence.finding: DistilBERT (BCE) micro-F1 0.632, macro-F1 0.589 on the SIAM 2007 test set (7,077 documents). No generative LLM was tested.

candidates.why_ft_beats_rag: Strong case on structure, not on facts. The flight phase and taxonomy labels are a mapping from narrative to a fixed code list, which retrieval over reports does not learn. Retrieval would only fix facts the model lacks; here the model needs to learn the coding rules.
candidates.example_input: Narrative (de-identified ASRS-style): 'During the taxi-out the first officer noticed the nosewheel steering light, the captain was distracted by a radio call and the aircraft was cleared for takeoff without the checklist being completed.'
candidates.example_output: {"flight_phase": "Taxi", "contributing_factors": ["Human Factors: distraction", "Procedure: checklist not completed"]}  (labels illustrative; the real code list comes from the ASRS taxonomy)
candidates.behavior_spec: Given one ASRS narrative, the model returns one valid JSON object with flight_phase drawn from the fixed phase list and contributing_factors drawn only from the taxonomy list; it reports each label that a trained analyst would assign and no labels outside the list, and it never adds prose.
candidates.agentic_demo: Step 1: a report intake service receives a narrative. Step 2: the SLM returns phase and factor codes as JSON. Step 3: a validator checks each code against the taxonomy list and rejects unknown labels. Step 4: a trend tool counts codes by month for a safety dashboard. Step 5: low-confidence records go to a human analyst queue.
candidates.eval: Per-label precision, recall and F1 against analyst labels, and exact-match on flight phase. Compare base, tuned, a prompted frontier model (zero-shot, few-shot, structured CoT) and the SafeAeroBERT baseline on the same held-out reports. The SafeAeroBERT figures above are the baseline to beat.
candidates.risks: Licence of the official data is unverified and bulk access is by request. Labels come from the ASRS coding taxonomy, and the public copies may not carry the contributing-factor fields. Narratives include personal details (de-identification needed). Human-factors labels are subjective, so inter-annotator agreement may set a low ceiling.
candidates.qlora_feasibility: Fits 4 days only if a dataset with contributing-factor labels is obtained quickly. The HF copy supports a flight-phase pilot now. Data prep effort is medium: taxonomy mapping, de-identification and checking labels against the NASA codebook.

candidates.name: Maintenance work order to failure-mode code (ISO 14224) and component/action extraction
candidates.industry: Industrial operations: mining, oil and gas, power, rail; asset maintenance and reliability engineering
candidates.task: Input: one maintenance work-order text (short free-text observation such as 'pump seal leaking, replaced'). Output: a failure-mode code from a fixed list of ISO 14224 failure modes, plus the component and maintenance action spans if the schema is extended.
candidates.why_hard_for_llm: The label set is fixed and domain-specific (22 ISO 14224 failure-mode codes). Stewart et al. (2023) report that GPT-3.5 without fine-tuning reaches F1 0.46 on this task, and with fine-tuning on 502 labelled pairs reaches F1 0.80 (the abstract says fine-tuned F1 = 0.80). Both models are GPT-3.5, so frontier-model reliability on this task is not yet tested.
candidates.business_value: Reliability engineers code failure modes by hand for FMEA, bad-actor analysis and warranty claims. Work orders are short and noisy, so a model that codes them to a standard code frees engineering time. Plant-level data stays on-site.

datasets.name: FMC-MWO2KG (failure-mode classification of maintenance observations)
datasets.size: 502 training, 62 validation, 62 test (paperswithcode listing; not verified against the dataset repo, the fetch failed on SSL)
datasets.labels: 22 ISO 14224 failure-mode codes, one per observation (expert-labelled)
datasets.license: Apache 2.0 (per a search summary of the paperswithcode listing; not read directly)
datasets.notes: Paper: MWO2KG and Echidna (Stewart, Hodkiewicz, Liu, French; Proc. IMechE Part O, 2024). Labels were taken from observations produced by an NER model and then corrected by hand. Test set of 62 gives wide confidence intervals; treat results as a pilot.

datasets.name: MaintIE (fine-grained annotation and benchmark for maintenance short texts)
datasets.size: 1,076 expert-annotated texts (gold; the repo's own section 3.4.2 says 1,067 double-annotated texts, a discrepancy) and 7,000 silver texts (repo, fetched)
datasets.labels: Entity and relation annotation, 5 top classes and 224 leaf entities (e.g. Item, Location, Observation, Specifier, Time). Not failure-mode codes directly.
datasets.notes: LREC-COLING 2024 paper (aclanthology 2024.lrec-main.954). Usable for component and action extraction; failure-mode mapping would need a new label layer.

frontier_evidence.source: Large Language Models for Failure Mode Classification: An Investigation (Stewart, Hodkiewicz, Li)
frontier_evidence.models_tested: GPT-3.5 (zero-shot, fine-tuned) and a conventional text classifier. No GPT-4 or newer model.
frontier_evidence.finding: Abstract (fetched): fine-tuned GPT-3.5 F1 = 0.80; conventional text classifier F1 = 0.60; out-of-the-box GPT-3.5 F1 = 0.46.

frontier_evidence.source: Aviation maintenance log structuring: GPT-4o vs fine-tuned small open models (PHM Asia-Pacific 2025)
frontier_evidence.models_tested: GPT-4o; Gemma-3-4B, LLaMA-3.2-3B, Phi-4-mini (instruct, after supervised fine-tuning)
frontier_evidence.finding: From a search summary, not read: fine-tuned Gemma-3-4B surpasses GPT-4o across multiple metrics. The task is abbreviation expansion and text generation, not failure-mode coding.

counterevidence.source: No newer LLM result on FMC-MWO2KG found in 2024-2025 searches
counterevidence.note: The 2023 GPT-3.5 result is the only one found. Frontier models may now do well with a good prompt and the 22-code list in context; the prompt-ceiling gate must test this first.

Entity-level NER on 224 fine-grained labels reaches only 64.43 micro-F1 for SpERT on 347 test entities (repo RESULTS.md, fetched). Fine-grained maintenance extraction is hard for an encoder too, so an SLM alone may not be enough.

small_model_evidence.finding: SpERT micro-F1 for NER: 89.88 with 1 class, 87.39 with 5 classes, 71.58 with 32 classes, 64.43 with 224 classes (fine-grained). Relation extraction strict F1 27.32 at 224 classes. These are encoder models, not small LLMs.

small_model_evidence.source: No small (<=8B) generative model evidence on FMC-MWO2KG found
small_model_evidence.finding: Gap: no paper found that fine-tunes a 1B-4B model on failure-mode coding.

candidates.why_ft_beats_rag: A fixed code list and noisy phrasing are a learned mapping. Retrieval helps only if similar past work orders carry the same code, which the 2023 study suggests is unreliable on short observations. Test this against a retrieval-few-shot baseline.
candidates.example_input: Work order text: 'Pump P-204 seal leaking at outboard side, changed mech seal, tested OK.'
candidates.example_output: {"failure_mode": "External leakage - process medium", "component": "mechanical seal", "action": "replace"}  (illustrative; the real code labels come from ISO 14224 as used in FMC-MWO2KG)
candidates.behavior_spec: Given one work-order observation text, the model returns one JSON object whose failure_mode is exactly one of the 22 ISO 14224 codes in the provided list; it returns the code a domain expert would assign for at least 80% of held-out observations and never invents a code outside the list.
candidates.agentic_demo: Step 1: a work-order export (CSV or CMMS API) feeds observation text. Step 2: the SLM returns failure-mode code and component. Step 3: a rule checks codes against the ISO 14224 list and flags unmatched text. Step 4: an FMEA table tool counts codes per asset class. Step 5: flagged records go to a reliability engineer.
candidates.eval: Macro-F1 and accuracy against expert labels on the FMC test split (62 items: report with a bootstrap CI, since n is small). Compare base 1.7B-4B, tuned, a prompted frontier model (zero-shot, few-shot, CoT with the code list), and the 2023 GPT-3.5 and text-classifier numbers as reference. Add the MaintIE NER spans for a component/action check.
candidates.risks: Dataset is small (502 train) and the test set has only 62 items, so differences of a few points are noise. Labels were partly derived from an NER model and corrected by hand. The licence has not been read at source. Data may come from a single industry partner, so transfer to other plants is unknown.
candidates.qlora_feasibility: Fits 4 days. Data is ready if the FMC repo and licence check out. Work is mostly format conversion and the frontier prompt-ceiling run. Judgement: 502 pairs is enough for a LoRA classifier pilot, not for a robust claim without a larger labelled set.

rejected.reason: Surfaced in a search only; not opened. Dated 2026 and may overlap the maintenance candidate. Worth checking later.
